newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh '97 grain harvest seen at 14 mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh '97 grain harvest seen at 14 mln tonnes.

text.p: Kazakhstan's 1997 grain harvest may be a net 14 million tonnes, up from last year's drought-hit 11.6 million, a senior analyst in the former Soviet republic said on Friday.

"According to this year's weather conditions, our scientists expect a harvest of 14 million tonnes, including some 11 million tonnes of wheat," Onal Shegebayev, director of the Kazakh Grain Farming Research Institute, told Reuters.
Shegebayev said he expected per hectare yields to average 0.8 tonnes across the 17 million hectares sown to grains this year.
"If we have rains this summer and a warm autumn, yields may rise to 1.1 tonnes per hectare," he said.
Last year's harvest was hit by a severe drought followed by rains and snow in September and October.
"This year's weather conditions seem to be better," Shegebayev said.
He said Kazakhstan's southern regions had begun harvesting barley, sown across five million ha.
The harvesting of spring wheat -- the country's main grain crop and sown across 10.5 million ha this year -- would start in late August or early September, to be completed by the end of September.
Shegebayev's grain institute -- located in in the heart of northern grain belt, 1,300 km from the capital Almaty -- was unique in the former Soviet Union.

Founded in 1956 during the Soviet "virgin lands" campaign, when Kazakhstan's marginal steppe land was ploughed up to boost grain production, the institute has specialised in cultivating new types of grain and improving farming techniques.
But Shegebayev said a lack of machinery, fuel and fertiliser had halved Kazakhstan's recent grain harvests from levels seen in Soviet times.
"Areas sown to grain have shrunk by 20 percent," he said. "Weeds alone consume up to 40 percent of the grain harvest each year."
Machinery depots at many local farms have an abandoned air, with tractors and combine harvesters rusting in deep grass.
"Due to falling yields, grain farming in Kazakhstan has become loss-making," Shegebayev said.
He said the hasty virgin lands campaign in Soviet times had led to soil erosion and environmental disaster in many regions.
"Around six million hectares -- mostly eroded or saline soils -- yield only 0.5-0.6 tonnes per hectare, and one cannot think of profitable grain farming there," he said.
But despite these problems Kazakhstan remains a major exporter of grain, especially to Russia.
"Kazakhstan exports four to five million tonnes of grain each year," Shegebayev said.
Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev told an investment summit earlier this month the Central Asian state might eventually export over 10 million tonnes of grain.
But Shegebayev's outlook was more cautious.
"For this, you need an annual output of 27-28 million tonnes," he said. "Taking into account the current situation, reaching this target will take many years."
